Topic: “It Don’t Mean a Thing If It Ain’t Got That Swing: Popular Music and Dance.” From the Charleston to “Hot to Go,” this course will provide students with an understanding of how popular music and iconic dances progress from marginalized communities to mainstream culture in the United States. Through critical case studies, students will get to know how racial and gender identities shape the creation and reception of music genres and dance trends, develop the skills to critically discuss and write about the intertextual relationship between sound and movement, and examine how media extracts practices from marginalized communities and reframe them to be accepted by mainstream American culture.

Topic: "HISTORY OF JAZZ." This course offers a chronological survey and analysis of various kinds of music that have been called jazz, from their nineteenth century roots to their contemporary expressions. We will take an expansive approach to the music. In addition to its history and practice in the United States, we will consider jazz’s connections to other styles (from the rhythms of Caribbean music to hip-hop and electronic music) and global reach. No previous musical knowledge is necessary.

sections.sectionText: Rubber Soul: Race, Genre, and the Sonic Politics of Rock ‘n’ Roll Rock music is Black music. Evolving out of the blues and, later, rhythm and blues, rock ‘n’ roll circa 1950s to early 1960s had a Black face, with artists like Chuck Berry and Little Richard leading the way. Yet, as rock ‘n’ roll gave way to rock during the second half of the 1960s, its Black origins were obscured, and rock culture became predominantly white. What were the cultural, historical, and sonic traditions that made rock ‘n’ roll possible? How did the erasure of Blacks from rock happen and why? What were the financial and cultural implications of that erasure? Students will learn about rock ‘n’ roll history, with an emphasis on rock from the 1960s and 1970s. Beginning in the 1920s and 1930s, with the sounds of delta and classic blues (Charley Patton, Bessie Smith) and early country too (Jimmie Rodgers, Bob Wills and His Texas Playboys), we will trace the arc of rock ‘n’ roll to rock, culminating with post-punk and the early-1980s, MTV era, second British Invasion (Duran Duran, Culture Club). Students will have the opportunity to write a short piece of rock criticism and a final seminar paper and presentation about a rock artist or an element of rock culture.

sections.sectionText: The Sacred Harp: the Performance and Politics of Shape-Note Singing Sacred Harp is a style of shape-note singing with histories in the American South and 18th– 19th century New England and the Mid-Atlantic. This class explores the complex histories, meanings, and performance of Sacred Harp and shape-note singing. Classes are divided between lecture-discussions and learning to sing Sacred Harp music in the traditional manner.

sections.sectionText: Black Music and Culture of the 1970s: The 1970s was—and remains—a key time period for understanding Black American musical and social life. This course will examine works by artists like Stevie Wonder, Aretha Franklin, and Marvin Gaye to understand the main musical ideas and social concerns of these artists and their audiences. Reading, listening, and discussion will focus on issues including the Civil Rights and Black Power movements, deindustrialization, technology, and the music industry. Our goal will be to build research and writing skills while studying this period. With our understanding of soul, funk, disco, jazz, and the beginnings of hip-hop, our final question will be: how and to what extent can we hear echoes of the Black music and culture of the 1970s in later decades and in our contemporary era?

sections.sectionText: Musical Theatre Repertoire is an asynchronous course, conducted by means of the interactive, video feedback platform GoReact. Fall semester is dedicated to the context, selection, and performance of Contemporary Musical Theatre Repertoire covering genres such as comedic/character selections, Sondheim, Disney, pop/rock, punk, country, disco, and motown. Spring semester is dedicated to pre-1970 musical theatre repertoire ranging from operetta through post-golden age repertoire. Feedback concerning vocal technique, musical and stylistic choices, and communication is given each week.

Topic: "BLACK SACRED MUSIC SYMPOSIUM XX." Instruction and experience in the performance of Black Sacred Music traditions such as congregational singing, folk and concert spirituals, metered and improvised hymns, anthems, and traditional and contemporary gospel songs. Topics include history and development, choral pedagogy, conducting, song selection, and vocal and instrumental performance techniques. Additionally, participants attend musical rehearsals and perform the repertoire learned during Symposium in a closing concert. The Eighteenth Black Sacred Music Symposium will be Thursday-Sunday, February 25-28, 2027.
CAPSTONE PROJECT SYNTHESIS.

Topic: "ENSEMBLE CREDIT - COLLABORATIVE PIANO AND CHAMBER MUSIC." Pianists only. Pianists work with ensembles, classes, and/or performances in the School of Music. Instructor Approval required, please see Dr. Chi-Chen Wu.

This course is designed to introduce and develop the essential skills for work as a music director in productions for the contemporary musical stage and high-level freelance work. Students will learn the rudiments of arranging and improvisation from a harmonic skeleton, become acquainted with the use of computers and stand-alone synthesizers, develop the skill of conducting from the keyboard, and attain basic familiarity with contemporary and classical musical theater vocal and instrumental styles. Students will prepare a musical to teach the class applying in a practical manner the skills studied. Excerpts from this musical will also be arranged for vocal and variable instrumental ensembles.

Topic: "ENSEMBLE CREDIT FOR PIANISTS - CHAMBER MUSIC AND ACCOMPANYING." Purpose of course / learning outcome: To actively participate in ensemble playing as a pianist, learning the associated skills, protocol and repertoire for specific use in collaborative settings including chamber music, vocal accompanying, choral accompanying, orchestral piano, dance class accompaniment or other activities as assigned. Procedures: In consultation with the instructor and other SoM or related faculty, the student will be assigned an activity. Examples: accompany a choir in rehearsal and performance, observe dance classes and then play classes at the instructor and supervisor’s discretion, accompany for a weekly voice lesson and select public performances with the singer, accompany for a portion of a solo degree recital or studio recital, participate as the pianist in an orchestra or band for one or more concerts and the appropriate rehearsals, etc.

sections.sectionText: Topic: "MUSIC TECH AND THE TRANSFORMATION OF AMERICAN LIFE, 1900-1930." Everyday experiences with sound and music in the U.S. underwent a profound transformation in the early twentieth century, largely due to three technologies: the phonograph, the radio, and the player piano. In this course, we will examine contemporary scholarship and evaluate a wide range of early twentieth-century primary sources—from player piano advertisements, to early examples of radio broadcast schedules, to transcripts of fiery congressional debates around copyright and recorded sound. These sources will foster seminar discussion of several key questions, including: How did the American public initially react to these three technologies? How did the way they were used change over the course of the early 20th century as they became integrated into everyday musical life? How did technological mediation—for example, the ability to capture music on a disc record or a piano roll—impact musical experiences, including music learning? What kinds of music and other programming were heard through these technologies, and who made the decisions? What ideas about race, gender, and class became mapped onto them, and which historical conditions contributed to this? As a part of this course, students will complete guided written reflections on assigned primary and secondary sources, as well as a final original research paper tied to one or more of the seminar’s central questions. COURSE IS ONLINE SYNCHRONOUS.

restrictions: Restricted to students with Graduate class standing.
sections.sectionText: The year 1927 will be the focal point for a wide-ranging seminar-style exploration of musical issues in America and Europe. A broad introduction will be followed by weekly case studies in which representative compositions and recordings help to bring key issues into focus: the clash and blend of musical idioms viewed as “high” and “low,” the impact of new technology (radio, sound film, electric recording) on musical creation and dissemination, machine aesthetics, urbanization, racial representations and assumptions; the co-existing aesthetics of neoclassicism, serialism, neue Sachlichkeit, varieties of American modernism, jazz, blues, spirituals, Broadway, popular song, and the Harlem Renaissance. Readings, listening, and discussion will drive class meetings, culminating in a final research project that intersects meaningfully with the year 1927.

sections.sectionText: “Sound and Coloniality” takes as its foundation an understanding of coloniality as the formations of knowledge and subjectivity, hierarchies, and social relations that sustain, reproduce, and outlast the colonial structures that generate them. The seminar draws on historical musicology, cultural history, sound studies, material culture, and decolonial studies to generate analytical frameworks to examine how colonized subjects negotiate, contest, appropriate and transform colonial systems through sonic and musical practices. The seminar welcomes participants from across disciplines interested in the critical study of sound and music; proficiency in musical notation or performance is not required.

sections.sectionText: Benjamin Britten envisioned music as emerging from the active participation of composers, performers, and audiences. In this course, we will explore the relationships Britten forged with these parties as well as his patrons and publishers on both sides of the Atlantic and the so-called “Iron Curtain;” the influences he gleaned from England, Europe, and East Asia; and the reception of his work including the controversies that arose after his death.
